units: a neighbor tells about a night of stargazing
the instrument was set up on a balcony late in the evening
she first mistook a fuzzy streak for a plane
the sky cleared afterwards
she recognized the comet that had been announced
she woke her brother, who grumbled before joining her
she noticed the object had shifted between two looks
she plans to go out again the next night better equipped
text: My neighbor was still laughing when she told me about her night of stargazing. She had set her instrument up on the balcony around dusk, while the sky was turning purple. For a good while, she said, she could make out nothing at all, just a fuzzy smear she took for a plane. Then the haze lifted, and that was when she caught her mistake: the pale streak she had been following for half an hour was the comet everyone had been waiting for. She shook her brother awake. He grumbled, then came out in his slippers, and the two of them watched the tail stretch above the rooftops. Toward the end she noticed the thing had crept a little to one side between one look and the next. She swore she would go back out the following night with hot tea and a blanket, since she had been shivering without noticing.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: glassworkers learned to polish even surfaces
the earliest instruments stopped distorting the images
stars invisible until then became observable
observers moved from description to measurement
star catalogs grew richer and more reliable
fuzzy patches turned out to be groups of stars
steadier mounts had to be built
precision machinery was born of that need
text: The steady improvement of lenses changed the study of the sky far beyond anything the craftsmen at the bench had in mind. Once glassworkers learned to polish a truly even surface, the earliest instruments stopped bending what they showed, and stars nobody had ever managed to see came into view. That sharpness had an immediate effect: observers gave up describing from memory and began to measure. Catalogs grew thicker and steadier, and faint smudges once lumped together turned out to be clusters of separate stars. Sturdier mounts had to be built next, because a trembling tube threw away everything the glass had gained. Out of that need grew a whole craft of precision machinery, with worm screws, gears and counterweights. Step by step, the glassworker's bench reshaped the way people questioned the night sky.

units: a diffuse glow hides the stars above built-up areas
the cause is lamplight aimed upward
particles hanging in the air scatter that light
faint stars become impossible to pick out
observers have to move away from towns
tilting the lamps toward the ground and capping them solves the problem
places that have applied this measure see their galaxy again
the measure also helps sleep, birds and spending
text: A milky pallor has settled over the sky of every built-up area, and the stars are vanishing under it one by one. The trouble comes from lamps that throw part of their beam upward, where the dust and damp hanging in the air scatter it. A halo forms above the streets, and the flicker of the faintest stars drowns in it. Anyone who still wants a dark vault overhead has to travel farther and farther from the towns. The cure exists and costs little: tilt the lamps toward the ground and cap them with an opaque hood. Small towns that have done so have watched the milky band of our galaxy return above their squares. Residents sleep less fitfully, migrating birds find their bearings once more, and the lighting bill drops. The black sky is not lost; it is waiting for someone to switch off.

units: a stockman brings in a dark stone found on his land
a specialist compares it with an already authenticated sample
the two lumps look alike on the outside
cutting them open reveals internal differences
the authenticated sample holds frozen droplets and metal
the stockman's stone holds only stretched cavities
it actually comes from foundry waste
magnetic pull explains the usual confusion
analysis of the metal content settled the question
text: A stockman brought a black stone into the laboratory, picked up in his own paddock and, he was sure, fallen from the sky. The technician set it beside a reference sample, a meteorite collected in a desert and long since logged. The two lumps looked like twins: dark crust, more heft than their bulk promised, blunted edges. Cutting them apart split their histories. The reference piece showed fine frozen droplets, the chondrules found in primitive rock, and a bright metal web that came out under polishing. The paddock stone held nothing but stretched bubbles, the mark of foundry slag chilled too fast. A magnet answered to both, which is why finders are so often misled. Only the ratio between two neighboring metals settled it, and the stockman went home with a piece of old industrial waste.

units: preparing a session follows a fixed order
power and backup lighting must be checked first
a red lamp keeps night vision from being spoiled
the optics must be aligned and cleaned before dark
the finder is set on a distant target while daylight lasts
the mount must stand on stable ground
the axis of the mount must point at the northern star
the observer must plan for clothing and a hot drink
the charts and lists are gathered last
text: Preparing an observing session works best in a fixed order. Power comes first: a charged battery, coiled cables, and a red-filtered lamp so that notes can be read without spoiling night vision. Optics come next, with the mirror aligned, the eyepieces wiped on a proper cloth, the finder trained on a distant landmark while daylight lasts. Then the mount: a tripod planted on firm ground, legs spread wide, its axis pointed at the northern star so that tracking stays even. Comfort deserves the same care, since sitting still chills a body faster than most people expect, so bring layered clothing, a hot drink and an adjustable seat. Paperwork is gathered last of all, sky chart, list of targets, notebook and pencil. A wasted session rarely comes down to the gear; it comes down to something forgotten in the rush out the door.

units: the craft left its parking orbit on an order from the ground
short bursts corrected a sideways drift
the views sent back first showed a gray cratered expanse
the ground proved rougher than expected
the original landing site was dropped during the descent
angular boulders covered the intended zone
a thin signal confirmed contact with the ground
the dust raised by the thrusters fell back without a cloud
drilling is announced after a recharging phase
text: The probe left its parking orbit shortly before dawn, on an order from the control center. All through the descent its thrusters fired in short bursts to trim a sideways drift spotted the day before. The first pictures sent back showed a gray plain pocked with shallow craters, then ground far rougher than anyone had planned for. Halfway down, the team gave up on the original landing site, since angular boulders littered the chosen patch. Touchdown was confirmed by a thin signal that arrived with the usual travel delay, and the room broke into applause. A side camera then filmed the dust kicked up by the nozzle, which fell straight back without forming a cloud. Drilling will begin after a rest period, officials said, because the lander must first recharge its batteries in the sun.

units: the crew spends its breaks at the observation window
the planet looks blue and streaked with white
the speed of the craft brings sunset back over and over
weightlessness sets loose objects drifting
every piece of equipment must be fastened or strapped down
the retreating water lays bare sandbars
the glazing is thick and built of several layers
a speck of dust at that speed would pierce an ordinary wall
passing into shadow causes condensation
text: Press your forehead against the window and you understand at once why the crew spends every one of its breaks here. Below you a blue marble keeps rolling past, streaked with white, close enough that you can trace the bends of the rivers. The craft moves so fast that sunset keeps coming back, so the sky catches fire, goes dark, and does it all over again. Inside, nothing falls. Weightlessness sends pens drifting to the ceiling, so every tool has to be strapped down or stuck to a magnet. Along one coast a paler fringe shows up, because the tide has pulled back and left sandbars bare. The glazing is thick, built in layers, since a speck of debris at this speed would punch through an ordinary wall. When the station slips into shadow the pane fogs over, and you wait for the warmth to come back.

units: low orbit is filling with dead craft and fragments
every fragment travels fast enough to pierce a wall
every collision breeds new fragments
some altitudes risk becoming unusable
the absence of a binding rule keeps up the inaction
every craft should carry the means to leave its orbit at end of life
a passive tracking device would make avoidance more reliable
recovery vehicles should capture the heavy wrecks
the cost of these measures is small next to the loss of access
text: Are we really going to wait for a major collision before anyone decides to act? Low orbit is filling up with wrecks: spent rocket stages, dead satellites, and shards thrown off by destructive tests. Every scrap travels fast enough to hole a wall, and every impact breeds more scraps, which threatens to put whole altitudes out of use. Operators pass the blame around, because no binding rule forces their hand. Three measures would turn the curve around. Require first that every craft carry enough propellant to drop out of orbit when its work is done. Impose next a passive tracking device, so that avoidance maneuvers stop resting on guesswork. Pay last for tugs able to grab the heaviest hulks. The bill looks steep; it is trivial next to an access our networks take for granted.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a keeper of the nebula register worked from a desk
her colleagues observed directly under the dome
clouds often cut their sessions short
she examined photographic plates through a magnifier
she measured the spread and the tint of the pale patches
her colleagues delivered impressions, she delivered measurements
a single plate took up a whole sitting
one scratch was enough to spoil the examination
she told two categories of fuzzy objects apart
those who came after inherited her classification
text: The woman who kept the register of nebulae hardly ever left her desk, and from there she saw farther than the colleagues posted under the dome. They watched the sky one night out of two, and the clouds spoiled a good part of it. She bent over photographic plates instead, comparing pale patches, measuring how far they spread, noting their tint through a magnifier. Where her fellows wrote down an impression, she wrote down a number. Her patience matched an embroiderer's, since one plate filled an entire sitting and a single scratch was enough to ruin the work. In the end she told two families of fuzzy objects apart, some woven of gas, others made of stars beyond counting. Those who came after her inherited a classification that nights under the dome would never have built.

units: the instrument tested belongs to the cheapest range
the mirror keeps stars sharp out to the edge of the field
the mount lacks mass and shakes at the slightest touch
every focus adjustment sets off a wobble to wait out
the eyepiece supplied gives a cramped field and a soft image
the optical diagonal throws unwanted reflections
the finder adjusts without tools and keeps its alignment
the manual says nothing about adjusting the mirrors
the verdict advises replacing the mount first
text: The budget instrument we tried deserves a part-by-part look, with no favors done. Start with the optics: the primary mirror holds an honest figure, and stars stay as points right out to the edge of the field, which is a surprise at this price. The mount is another matter, far too light, shivering at the slightest touch, and every turn of the focuser sets off a wobble you have to wait out. The extras disappoint. The bundled eyepiece gives a cramped field and a soft image, while the diagonal throws stray reflections across bright stars. The finder, though, adjusts without tools and keeps its aim from one night to the next. Then the manual, rushed through translation, silent on collimating the mirrors, which the buyer will face in the first week. Verdict: a decent tube on a mount that cannot hold it.
